annotation.targetText: Capital itself is the moving contradiction, [in] that it presses to reduce labour time to a minimum, while it posits labour time, on the other side, as sole measure and source of wealth.
annotation.summary: Capitalism contains a fundamental contradiction regarding technology: it uses automation to reduce the necessary labor time required to produce goods, yet continues to measure human worth and income strictly by hours worked.
annotation.explanation: Capitalism contains a fundamental contradiction regarding technology: it uses automation to reduce the necessary labor time required to produce goods, yet continues to measure human worth and income strictly by hours worked.

annotation.targetText: Production becomes social, but appropriation remains private.
annotation.summary: Modern production relies on global supply chains and millions of coordinated workers (socialized production), but the profits and ownership remain locked in the hands of a small group of private investors (private appropriation).
annotation.explanation: Modern production relies on global supply chains and millions of coordinated workers (socialized production), but the profits and ownership remain locked in the hands of a small group of private investors (private appropriation).
annotation.context: This is a core structural contradiction of capitalism: society functions as an interconnected web of collective labor, but private capitalists retain exclusive ownership and decision-making power over the resulting wealth.

annotations.bookTitle: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism
annotations.chapterTitle: I. Concentration of Production and Monopolies

annotation.targetText:
concentration of production and capital has developed to
 such a high stage that it has created monopolies
annotation.summary: Capitalist competition naturally leads to concentration, which inevitably creates monopolies that dominate all major sectors of economic life.
annotation.explanation: Capitalist competition naturally leads to concentration, which inevitably creates monopolies that dominate all major sectors of economic life.
annotation.context: This refutes idealist theories that capitalism can return to 19th-century small-business competition. Monopolies are an organic and permanent outcome of capitalist growth.

annotations.bookTitle: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism
annotations.chapterTitle: VII. Imperialism as a Special Stage of Capitalism

annotation.targetText: There is no doubt that the development is going in the direction of a single world trust that will swallow up all enterprises and all states without exception. But the development in this direction is proceeding under such stress, with such a tempo, with such contradictions, conflicts, and convulsions-not only economical, but also political, national, etc., etc.-that before a single world trust will be reached, before the respective national finance capitals will have formed a world union of "ultra-imperialism," imperialism will inevitably explode, capitalism will turn into its opposite.
annotation.summary: Before global capitalism could ever unite into Kautsky's peaceful 'single world trust', its violent contradictions will cause imperialism to explode in socialist revolution.
annotation.explanation: Lenin refutes Karl Kautsky's reformist dream of 'ultra-imperialism', demonstrating that the uneven, catastrophic development of monopoly capitalism intensifies wars and class struggles long before a global monopoly could peacefully consolidate.

annotation.targetText: The fact is that the very foundation of modern states as definite political entities was caused by economic needs and requirements. The state grew on the economic foundation; it was only an expression of economic connections; state ties appeared only as an expression of economic ties.
annotation.summary: Contrary to idealist theories of the 'state principle', modern nation-states emerged as political expressions of underlying capitalist economic ties.
annotation.explanation: Bukharin applies historical materialism to refute bourgeois state idealism, demonstrating that the national state arose to consolidate and protect the economic connections of the national bourgeoisie.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.chapterTitle: Ch. IV: The Inner Structure of "National Economies" and the Tariff Policy

annotation.targetText:
We have laid bare three fundamental motives for the conquest policies of modern capitalist states: increased competition in the sales markets, in the markets of raw materials, and for the spheres of capital investment. This is what the modern development of capitalism and its transformation into finance capitalism has brought about.

Those three roots of the policy of finance capitalism, however, represent in substance only three facets of the same phenomenon, namely of the conflict between the growth of productive forces on the one hand, and the "national" limits of the production organisation on the other.
annotation.summary: The three drivers of imperialist conquest (sales markets, raw materials, and capital investment spheres) stem from the conflict between global productive forces and national bourgeois states.
annotation.explanation: Bukharin synthesizes his theory of imperialism: productive forces have outgrown the narrow framework of the nation-state, forcing finance capital to attempt to resolve the contradiction through military conquest.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.chapterTitle: Ch. VIII: World Economy and the "National" State

annotation.targetText: Hegel's dialectics, which Marx placed on its feet, is valuable for this very reason that it grasps the dialectics of life, that it fearlessly analyses the present without being disturbed by the fact that every existence hides within itself the germ of its own destruction.
annotation.summary: Placed on materialist feet by Marx, dialectics reveals that every historical social form contains the internal contradictions that lead to its overthrow.
annotation.explanation: Contrasting Marx's materialist dialectic with Hegel's mystified idealist form, Bukharin concludes that the sharpening contradictions of finance capitalism inevitably prepare the bursting of the capitalist shell.

annotation.targetText: Our “Left” Communists, however, who are also fond of calling themselves “proletarian” Communists, because there is very little that is proletarian about them and very much that is petty-bourgeois, are incapable of giving thought to the balance of forces, to calculating it. This is the core of Marxism and Marxist tactics, but they disdainfully brush aside the “core” with “proud” phrases
annotation.summary: Calculating the objective material balance of class forces is the core of Marxist tactics, whereas ultra-leftism substitutes subjective phrases for material reality.
annotation.explanation: Lenin exposes the philosophical idealism and petty-bourgeois class character of ultra-leftism: instead of analyzing real material and military conditions, Left Communists treat their own subjective revolutionary desires as sufficient.

annotations.chapterTitle: I. The Brest Peace and the Balance of Forces

annotation.targetText: For our “Lefts” merely brandish a cardboard sword when they ignore the universally known fact, of which the war in the Ukraine has served as an additional proof, that peoples utterly exhausted by three years of butchery cannot go on fighting without a respite; and that war, if it cannot be organised on a national scale, very often creates a mentality of disintegration peculiar to petty proprietors, instead of the iron discipline of the proletariat.
annotation.summary: Ignoring the material exhaustion of the masses to demand immediate 'revolutionary war' is brandishing a cardboard sword.
annotation.explanation: Lenin contrasts proletarian discipline grounded in the real material conditions of working people with the aristocratic idealism of petty-bourgeois intellectuals who despise the war-weary masses' need for a breathing space.

annotations.chapterTitle: I. The Brest Peace and the Balance of Forces

annotation.targetText: I shall enlighten you, my amiable friends, as to why such disaster overtook you. It is because you devote more effort to learning by heart and committing to memory revolutionary slogans than to thinking them out.
annotation.summary: Dogmatism memorizes revolutionary slogans from the past instead of dialectically analyzing changed historical conditions.
annotation.explanation: Lenin critiques the Left Communists for repeating yesterday's anti-defencist slogans by rote without recognizing that the proletariat's seizure of state power fundamentally changed the class nature of defending the country.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.chapterTitle: II. Proletarian Defencism and Revolutionary Phrase-Making

annotation.targetText: At present, petty-bourgeois capitalism prevails in Russia, and it is one and the same road that leads from it to both large-scale state capitalism and to socialism, through one and the same intermediary station called “national accounting and control of production and distribution”. Those who fail to understand this are committing an unpardonable mistake in economics. Either they do not know the facts of life, do not see what actually exists and are unable to look the truth in the face, or they confine themselves to abstractly comparing “capitalism” with “socialism” and fail to study the concrete forms and stages of the transition that is taking place in our country.
annotation.summary: Abstractly counterposing 'capitalism' and 'socialism' ignores the concrete material intermediary stages required to transition from small-scale production to socialism.
annotation.explanation: Lenin critiques the idealist method of the Left Communists, who compare abstract concepts of capitalism and socialism in their heads instead of studying the real material pathway of national accounting and control.

annotations.chapterTitle: IV. Large-Scale Engineering and National Accounting

annotation.targetText: On the one hand, it would be a fatal mistake to declare that since there is a discrepancy between our economic “forces” and our political strength, it “follows” that we should not have seized power.[4] Such an argument can be advanced only by a “man in a muffler”,[5] who forgets that there will always be such a “discrepancy”, that it always exists in the development of nature as well as in the development of society, that only by a series of attempts: each of which, taken by itself, will be one sided and will suffer from certain inconsistencies: will complete socialism be created by the revolutionary co-operation of the proletarians of all countries.
annotation.summary: Refusing to seize political power until economic conditions are 'perfect' is mechanical dogmatism; uneven development is universal in nature and history.
annotation.explanation: Lenin refutes both Menshevik determinism (which claimed Russia was too economically backward for revolution) and ultra-left impatience, showing that proletarian state power can be used to consciously accelerate material development.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.chapterTitle: V. Compromises, Labour Discipline, and Socialist Construction

annotation.targetText: No. Only those are worthy of the name of Communists who understand that it is impossible to create or introduce socialism without learning from the organisers of the trusts. For socialism is not a figment of the imagination, but the assimilation and application by the proletarian vanguard, which has seized power, of what has been created by the trusts.
annotation.summary: Socialism is not an idealist figment of the imagination, but the working class's practical appropriation and mastery of large-scale organization created by capitalism.
annotation.explanation: Against the idealist fantasy that socialism can be invented out of pure revolutionary willpower without technical expertise, Lenin insists that the proletarian state must employ and learn from first-class technical specialists under workers' oversight.

annotations.chapterTitle: V. Compromises, Labour Discipline, and Socialist Construction

annotation.targetText:
The law of contradiction in things, that is, the law of the unity of opposites,
is the basic law of materialist dialectics.
annotation.summary: Change happens because everything contains opposing forces pushing against each other. For example, a business grows through the tension between keeping prices low for customers and earning enough profit to pay workers and upgrade tools.
annotation.explanation: Change happens because everything contains opposing forces pushing against each other. For example, a business grows through the tension between keeping prices low for customers and earning enough profit to pay workers and upgrade tools.

annotation.targetText:
The metaphysical or vulgar evolutionist world outlook sees things as isolated,
static and one-sided.
annotation.summary: Metaphysical and idealist philosophy views things as isolated, static, and unchanged by internal contradictions.
annotation.explanation: Metaphysical thinking assumes things stay fixed and act independently. For example, treating a failing student as simply 'lazy' ignores their health, study environment, and home life, reducing a complex person to a single fixed trait.

annotation.targetText:
The universality or absoluteness of contradiction has a twofold meaning.
One is that contradiction exists in the process of development of all things,
and the other is that in the process of development of each thing a movement
of opposites exists from beginning to end.
annotation.summary: Tension and opposing forces exist in everything, from science to human relationships, from the moment something begins until it ends. Real-life example: In physical fitness, building muscle requires breaking down muscle fibers through stress so they grow back stronger. Tension exists from start to finish.
annotation.explanation: Tension and opposing forces exist in everything, from science to human relationships, from the moment something begins until it ends. Real-life example: In physical fitness, building muscle requires breaking down muscle fibers through stress so they grow back stronger. Tension exists from start to finish.

annotation.targetText:
There is nothing that does not contain contradiction;
without contradiction nothing would exist.
annotation.summary: Nothing in the universe is completely static or without internal tension. Real-life example: An ecosystem exists only because predators and prey, plants and soil nutrients continuously interact and balance against each other.
annotation.explanation: Nothing in the universe is completely static or without internal tension. Real-life example: An ecosystem exists only because predators and prey, plants and soil nutrients continuously interact and balance against each other.

annotation.targetText:
Opposition and struggle between ideas of different kinds constantly occur
within the Party; this is a reflection within the Party of contradictions
between classes and between the new and the old in society.
annotation.summary: Disagreements inside a team or political group are not random mistakes; they reflect real competing pressures from the broader world. Real-life example: In a community group, debates between members who want immediate spending versus long-term saving reflect real economic pressures facing different households.
annotation.explanation: Disagreements inside a team or political group are not random mistakes; they reflect real competing pressures from the broader world. Real-life example: In a community group, debates between members who want immediate spending versus long-term saving reflect real economic pressures facing different households.

annotation.targetText:
Every form of motion contains within itself its own particular
contradiction. This particular contradiction constitutes the particular essence
which distinguishes one thing from another.
annotation.summary: Every field or subject has its own unique conflict that makes it what it is. Physics focuses on force vs. resistance; economics focuses on supply, demand, and labor value; personal relationships focus on intimacy vs. independence.
annotation.explanation: Every field or subject has its own unique conflict that makes it what it is. Physics focuses on force vs. resistance; economics focuses on supply, demand, and labor value; personal relationships focus on intimacy vs. independence.

annotation.targetText:
Qualitatively different contradictions can only be resolved by qualitatively
different methods.
annotation.summary: Different problems require completely different solutions. Real-life example: You fix a broken car engine with mechanical tools, but you fix a broken friendship with open conversation and empathy. Trying to fix a friendship with mechanical tools will only cause harm.
annotation.explanation: Different problems require completely different solutions. Real-life example: You fix a broken car engine with mechanical tools, but you fix a broken friendship with open conversation and empathy. Trying to fix a friendship with mechanical tools will only cause harm.

annotation.targetText:
Hence, if in any process there are a number of contradictions, one of them
must be the principal contradiction playing the leading and decisive role,
while the rest occupy a secondary and subordinate position.
annotation.summary: When facing multiple problems at once, one main problem controls all the others. Real-life example: If a roof is leaking during a storm, fixing squeaky floorboards can wait; fixing the leak is the main problem that must be solved first.
annotation.explanation: When facing multiple problems at once, one main problem controls all the others. Real-life example: If a roof is leaking during a storm, fixing squeaky floorboards can wait; fixing the leak is the main problem that must be solved first.

annotations.chapterTitle: IV. THE PRINCIPAL CONTRADICTION AND THE PRINCIPAL ASPECT OF A CONTRADICTION

annotation.targetText:
The principal aspect is the one playing the leading
role in the contradiction. The nature of a thing is determined mainly by
the principal aspect of a contradiction, the aspect which has gained the
dominant position.
annotation.summary: Inside any conflict between two sides, whichever side holds power right now defines what the situation currently looks like. Real-life example: In a sports game, if one team controls the ball 80% of the time, their playing style dictates the whole match.
annotation.explanation: Inside any conflict between two sides, whichever side holds power right now defines what the situation currently looks like. Real-life example: In a sports game, if one team controls the ball 80% of the time, their playing style dictates the whole match.

annotations.chapterTitle: IV. THE PRINCIPAL CONTRADICTION AND THE PRINCIPAL ASPECT OF A CONTRADICTION

annotation.targetText:
Contradiction and struggle are universal and absolute,
but the methods of resolving contradictions, that is, the forms of struggle,
differ according to the differences in the nature of the contradictions.
annotation.summary: Because conflicts vary in nature, your method of solving them must fit the situation. Real-life example: Differences of opinion among project teammates are resolved through discussion, while structural wage theft requires collective union action or legal pressure.
annotation.explanation: Because conflicts vary in nature, your method of solving them must fit the situation. Real-life example: Differences of opinion among project teammates are resolved through discussion, while structural wage theft requires collective union action or legal pressure.

annotations.chapterTitle: VI. THE PLACE OF ANTAGONISM IN CONTRADICTION

annotation.targetText:
Lenin said, "Antagonism and contradiction are not at all one and the same.
Under socialism, the first will disappear, the second will remain."
annotation.summary: Lenin points out that even in a fair society without exploitation, people will still face challenges, decisions, and debates that drive progress. Real-life example: Even in a close-knit family, members will disagree on house design or budgeting, but those problems are solved through discussion rather than hostility.
annotation.explanation: Lenin points out that even in a fair society without exploitation, people will still face challenges, decisions, and debates that drive progress. Real-life example: Even in a close-knit family, members will disagree on house design or budgeting, but those problems are solved through discussion rather than hostility.

annotations.chapterTitle: VI. THE PLACE OF ANTAGONISM IN CONTRADICTION

annotation.targetText:
The law of contradiction in things,
that is, the law of the unity of opposites, is the fundamental law of nature
and of society and therefore also the fundamental law of thought.
annotation.summary: Mao summarizes that opposing forces drive everything: physical forces in nature, human history, and thoughts in our minds. Real-life example: Understanding this helps us stay calm during big life changes, knowing that tension and conflict are normal parts of growth.
annotation.explanation: Mao summarizes that opposing forces drive everything: physical forces in nature, human history, and thoughts in our minds. Real-life example: Understanding this helps us stay calm during big life changes, knowing that tension and conflict are normal parts of growth.

annotation.targetText:
In studying the particularity and relativity
of contradiction, we must give attention to the distinction between the principal
contradiction and the non-principal contradictions and to the distinction
between the principal aspect and the non-principal aspect of a contradiction
annotation.summary: Solving real-world problems requires separating the main issue from side issues, and recognizing which force holds power right now. Real-life example: A manager who focuses on office decorations while sales drop is failing to separate principal from non-principal issues.
annotation.explanation: Solving real-world problems requires separating the main issue from side issues, and recognizing which force holds power right now. Real-life example: A manager who focuses on office decorations while sales drop is failing to separate principal from non-principal issues.

annotation.targetText: The Marxist philosophy of dialectical materialism has two outstanding characteristics. One is its class nature: it openly avows that dialectical materialism is in the service of the proletariat. The other is its practicality: it emphasizes the dependence of theory on practice, emphasizes that theory is based on practice and in turn serves practice.
annotation.summary: Marxist dialectical materialism is defined by two core features: its open class allegiance to the working class, and its practical foundation where theory arises from and guides practice.
annotation.explanation: Unlike bourgeois academic philosophy, which pretends to stand neutrally above classes while defending capitalist social relations, Marxist dialectical materialism openly declares its partisan class standpoint on behalf of the working class and insists that philosophical truth is measured by its practical capacity to emancipate humanity.
annotation.context: Western Neo-Marxist academic departments deliberately severed Marxist theory from working-class political organization, turning it into neutral university seminar commentary divorced from practical struggle.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: If you want knowledge, you must take part in the practice of changing reality. If you want to know the taste of a pear, you must change the pear by eating it yourself.
annotation.summary: Genuine knowledge cannot be gained by passive observation; you can only discover the true nature of reality by actively participating in changing it.
annotation.explanation: Using one of his most famous everyday metaphors, Mao illustrates the materialist principle that genuine knowledge cannot be gained through passive contemplation or armchair speculation; one can only uncover the internal properties and laws of an object by actively interacting with and transforming it.
annotation.context: Labor organizers cannot understand the concrete contradictions of a workplace merely by reading sociological reports; they uncover the real power dynamics only by organizing alongside workers on the shop floor.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: Anyone who thinks that rational knowledge need not be derived from perceptual knowledge is an idealist. In the history of philosophy there is the "rationalist" school that admits the reality only of reason and not of experience, believing that reason alone is reliable while perceptual experience is not; this school errs by turning things upside down.
annotation.summary: Theories and rational concepts do not drop from the sky; they must be grounded in direct practical experience and concrete investigation, or else they fall into philosophical idealism.
annotation.explanation: Mao critiques philosophical idealism and dogmatic rationalism for treating abstract concepts as self-generated truths independent of material sense experience. Without concrete investigation of material conditions, abstract theories become 'water without a source, a tree without roots.'
annotation.context: Dogmatic sectarians who attempt to apply memorized formulas from another century without investigating current economic data or working-class conditions fall into idealist rationalism.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: We are also opposed to "Left" phrase-mongering. The thinking of "Leftists" outstrips a given stage of development of the objective process; some regard their fantasies as truth, while others strain to realize in the present an ideal which can only be realized in the future. They alienate themselves from the current practice of the majority of the people and from the realities of the day, and show themselves adventurist in their actions.
annotation.summary: Ultra-leftism detaches revolutionary desires from current material conditions and mass consciousness, mistaking wishful fantasies for immediate reality and leading to reckless adventurism.
annotation.explanation: Mao provides a sharp epistemological diagnosis of ultra-leftism: whereas Right opportunists lag behind objective reality, ultra-leftists detach their subjective desires from the actual material stage of development and the consciousness of the masses, substituting revolutionary-sounding slogans and reckless adventurism for patient mass organization.
annotation.context: Small ultra-left sects that reject united-front coalitions or trade union struggles because those struggles do not immediately abolish capitalism isolate themselves from the working class.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: Discover the truth through practice, and again through practice verify and develop the truth. Start from perceptual knowledge and actively develop it into rational knowledge; then start from rational knowledge and actively guide revolutionary practice to change both the subjective and the objective world. Practice, knowledge, again practice, and again knowledge.
annotation.summary: Human knowledge develops in an endless upward spiral: starting from practical experience, rising to rational theory, and returning to revolutionary practice to test and deepen truth.
annotation.explanation: Mao's concluding synthesis encapsulates the entire Marxist-Leninist theory of knowledge. Truth is not a static dogma achieved once and for all, but a continuous, upward-spiraling cycle in which practical struggle generates theoretical insight, and theoretical insight guides higher levels of revolutionary practice.
annotation.context: In socialist economic planning and community organizing, policies are formulated from concrete surveys, tested in pilot programs, evaluated against real-world outcomes, and refined for broader implementation.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Relation Between Knowledge and Practice, Between Knowing and Doing

annotation.targetText: All the experience of the ten months of war proves the error both of the theory of China's inevitable subjugation and of the theory of China's quick victory. The former gives rise to the tendency to compromise and the latter to the tendency to underestimate the enemy. Both approaches to the problem are subjective and one-sided, or, in a word, unscientific.
annotation.summary: Both the belief that China is doomed to lose and the belief that China will win quickly are unscientific errors that focus on only one side of reality.
annotation.explanation: Mao applies materialist dialectics to critique two opposite forms of subjectivism: capitulationist pessimism, which sees only Japan's military strength, and rash optimism, which ignores China's material weaknesses after isolated tactical victories.
annotation.context: In any long liberation or labor struggle, exaggerating the opponent's power leads to surrender, while underestimating their resources after a single win leads to reckless defeat.

annotation.targetText: Thus it can be seen that Japan has great military, economic and political-organizational power, but that her war is reactionary and barbarous, her manpower and material resources are inadequate, and she is in an unfavourable position internationally. China, on the contrary, has less military, economic and political-organizational power, but she is in her era of progress, her war is progressive and just, she is moreover a big country, a factor which enables her to sustain a protracted war, and she will be supported by most countries.
annotation.summary: Japan is militarily strong today, but its war is unjust, its resources are limited, and it is isolated abroad; China is militarily weak today, but its cause is just, its territory and population are vast, and the world supports its struggle.
annotation.explanation: Rather than comparing weapon counts in isolation, Mao analyzes the totality of political, economic, geographic, and international contradictions governing both belligerents, proving why China cannot win quickly but cannot be defeated.
annotation.context: This dialectical framework later explained how anti-colonial movements in Vietnam and Algeria defeated wealthier, heavily armed imperialist powers.

annotation.targetText: Do we deny the danger of national subjugation? No, we do not. We recognize that China faces two possible prospects, liberation or subjugation, and that the two are in violent conflict. Our task is to achieve liberation and to avert subjugation.
annotation.summary: Dialectical analysis neither ignores the real danger of defeat nor treats defeat as inevitable; instead, it identifies the concrete conditions needed to turn the possibility of liberation into reality.
annotation.explanation: Mao contrasts materialist dialectics with both fatalistic pessimism and blind optimism: both liberation and subjugation exist as competing possibilities, and conscious struggle determines which side prevails.
annotation.context: Unlike Kuomintang defeatists who saw only China's weaknesses or rash optimists who ignored them, the Communist Party analyzed how to actively build the conditions for victory.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Theory of National Subjugation Is Wrong and the Theory of Quick Victory Is Likewise Wrong

annotation.targetText: The enemy is strong and we are weak, and the danger of subjugation is there. But in other respects the enemy has shortcomings and we have advantages. The enemy's advantage can be reduced and his shortcomings aggravated by our efforts. On the other hand, our advantages can be enhanced and our shortcoming remedied by our efforts.
annotation.summary: Because strength and weakness are relative rather than fixed, sustained struggle can wear down the enemy's initial military advantage while multiplying the people's political and geographic advantages.
annotation.explanation: Mao explains why the war must be protracted: it takes time and persistent effort to erode Japan's military superiority and develop China's latent advantages to the point where the balance of power flips.
annotation.context: Even while Western corporations continued selling war materials to Japan in 1938, prolonged Chinese resistance steadily drained Japan's finances and manpower.

annotation.targetText: The first stage covers the period of the enemy's strategic offensive and our strategic defensive. The second stage will be the period of the enemy's strategic consolidation and our preparation for the counter-offensive. The third stage will be the period of our strategic counter-offensive and the enemy's strategic retreat.
annotation.summary: The protracted war unfolds in three stages: defending against the enemy's initial offensive, wearing the enemy down during a long stalemate, and launching the final counter-offensive.
annotation.explanation: Mao maps the dialectical transformation of the war from strategic defensive through prolonged stalemate to strategic counter-offensive, explaining how guerrilla and mobile warfare gradually shift China from inferiority to parity and finally superiority.
annotation.context: The Sino-Japanese War from 1937 to 1945 followed this exact trajectory: rapid Japanese advances into 1938, a prolonged stalemate with vast rural guerrilla bases from 1939 to 1944, and the final counter-offensive in 1945.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Three Stages of the Protracted War

annotation.targetText: Thus there are two forms of encirclement by the enemy forces and two forms of encirclement by our own: rather like a game of weichi. [16] Campaigns and battles fought by the two sides resemble the capturing of each other's pieces, and the establishment of enemy strongholds (such as Talyuan) and our guerrilla base areas (such as the Wutai Mountains) resembles moves to dominate spaces on the board.
annotation.summary: Although Japan surrounds China strategically, China's rural guerrilla bases surround Japan's occupied cities and railways from the outside, just like surrounding stones in a game of Go.
annotation.explanation: Mao uses the board game weichi (Go) to illustrate how an invader that strategically encircles China on a map is simultaneously counter-encircled on the ground by rural guerrilla base areas surrounding every occupied city and railway.
annotation.context: Japanese forces held major cities like Taiyuan and railway lines, but could not step into the surrounding countryside controlled by Eighth Route Army base areas.

annotation.targetText: Ideas, etc. are subjective, while deeds or actions are the subjective translated into the objective, but both represent the dynamic role peculiar to human beings. We term this kind of dynamic role "man's conscious dynamic role", and it is a characteristic that distinguishes man from all other beings.
annotation.summary: While material conditions set the stage and limits of what is possible, conscious human action and strategy are required to turn the possibility of victory into reality.
annotation.explanation: Mao distinguishes dialectical materialism from mechanical fatalism: objective conditions do not automatically produce victory without human agency, planning, and active struggle grounded in objective facts.
annotation.context: Even when an economic crisis weakens the ruling class, social change does not happen automatically unless workers consciously organize and act.

annotation.targetText: It can therefore be said that politics is war without bloodshed while war is politics with bloodshed.
annotation.summary: Politics is conflict without bloodshed, and war is political conflict carried out through bloodshed.
annotation.explanation: Mao condenses the Marxist theory of war: armed conflict is not a purely technical military exercise divorced from class and national politics, but the continuation of political struggle when obstacles cannot be removed by peaceful means.
annotation.context: An army that treats war as purely a matter of weapons and ignores the political needs of the population inevitably loses popular support.

annotation.targetText: The object of war, namely, the preservation of oneself and the destruction of the enemy, is the essence of war and the basis of all war activities, an essence which pervades all war activities, from the technical to the strategic.
annotation.summary: Every military tactic and strategy boils down to two interrelated goals: preserving one's own forces and destroying the enemy's capacity to resist.
annotation.explanation: Mao traces the dialectical unity of attack and defence from the ancient spear and shield to modern warfare: attack (destroying the enemy) is the primary means of self-preservation, while defence and partial sacrifice serve the preservation of the whole.
annotation.context: Whether a soldier takes cover while firing or a field army retreats to set up an ambush, both actions combine self-preservation with disarming the enemy.

annotation.targetText: In the first and second stages of the war, i.e., in the stages of the enemy's offensive and preservation of his gains, we should conduct tactical offensives within the strategic defensive, campaigns and battles of quick decision within the strategically protracted war, and campaigns and battles on exterior lines within strategically interior lines.
annotation.summary: Within a long defensive war, a weaker army wins by concentrating superior numbers to launch fast, offensive encirclements in individual battles.
annotation.explanation: Mao demonstrates the dialectical inversion between strategy and tactics: strategically China defends over a long war, but tactically on each battlefield China concentrates several divisions against one moving Japanese column to win swift offensive victories.
annotation.context: At the Battle of Pinghsingkuan, the Eighth Route Army ambushed and wiped out an advancing Japanese supply column swiftly before reinforcements could arrive.

annotations.chapterTitle: Offence Within Defence, Quick Decisions Within a Protracted War, Exterior Lines Within Interior Lines

annotation.targetText: The initiative here means an army's freedom of action as distinguished from an enforced loss of freedom. Freedom of action is the very life of an army and, once it is lost, the army is close to defeat or destruction.
annotation.summary: In warfare, the initiative means maintaining freedom of action; a weaker force wrests the initiative from a stronger invader through local superiority, deception, surprise attacks, and mass support.
annotation.explanation: Mao demonstrates that material superiority does not automatically confer the initiative: by organizing the local population to blind the enemy's intelligence and striking unprepared columns, an inferior army forces a superior invader into passivity.
annotation.context: In the anti-Japanese base areas, armed villagers blocked information leaks so effectively that Japanese columns repeatedly marched into Eighth Route Army ambushes.

annotation.targetText: In the great river of absolute fluidity throughout the war there is relative stability at each particular stretch: such is our fundamental view regarding war plans or policies.
annotation.summary: Although battlefield conditions constantly shift, military and political strategy requires plans that remain relatively stable throughout each specific stage of development.
annotation.explanation: Mao applies the dialectical unity of absolute motion and relative rest to strategic planning, refuting both rigid dogmatists who never adapt plans and relativists who reject planning altogether.
annotation.context: While tactical battle plans changed several times a day, the Eighth Route Army's overarching strategic policy of guerrilla and mobile warfare remained stable throughout an entire phase of the war.

annotation.targetText: Hence campaigns of annihilation are the means of attaining the objective of strategic attrition. In this sense war of annihilation is war of attrition. It is chiefly by using the method of attrition through annihilation that China can wage protracted war.
annotation.summary: A weaker nation wears down a powerful invader strategically (war of attrition) by concentrating forces to wipe out isolated enemy units in individual battles (battles of annihilation).
annotation.explanation: Mao resolves the apparent contradiction between attrition and annihilation: fighting purely defensive battles of attrition drains China's own scarce resources, whereas swiftly encircling and annihilating small enemy columns depletes the enemy while replenishing Chinese arms and morale.
annotation.context: Capturing rifles, artillery, and supplies in short encirclement battles allowed the Eighth Route Army to arm itself directly from Japanese transport columns.

annotations.chapterTitle: War of Attrition and War of Annihilation

annotation.targetText: The landlord class, the bourgeoisie and the warlords of Japan have very serious internal contradictions, which are growing, and the lack of military co-ordination is one of the concrete manifestations of this fact.
annotation.summary: Imperialist powers are never monolithic; internal rivalries among their ruling landlord, capitalist, and military factions inevitably produce strategic blunders that revolutionary forces can exploit.
annotation.explanation: Mao identifies five major operational errors committed by the Japanese command (piecemeal reinforcement, no main direction of attack, lack of coordination, missed opportunities, and failure to annihilate), tracing them to Japan's class contradictions and troop shortages.
annotation.context: Fierce rivalries between Japanese army factions in northern and central China repeatedly prevented coordinated offensives and left vast rural areas unguarded.

annotations.chapterTitle: The Possibilities of Exploiting the Enemy's Mistakes

annotation.targetText: In the eyes of the subjugationists the enemy are supermen and we Chinese are worthless, while in the eyes of the theorists of quick victory we Chinese are supermen and the enemy are worthless. Both are wrong. We take a different view; the War of Resistance Against Japan is a protracted war, and the final victory will be China's.
annotation.summary: Defeatists treat the enemy as invincible supermen while quick-victory dreamers treat the enemy as helpless; realistic materialist analysis shows the war will be long, hard, and ultimately victorious.
annotation.explanation: Mao concludes his lectures by contrasting metaphysical extremes with materialist dialectics, which assesses both the enemy's temporary strength and its fatal long-term contradictions.
annotation.context: Delivered in May and June 1938, Mao's strategic blueprint guided the Chinese resistance through seven more years of war to victory in August 1945.

annotation.targetText: We are confronted with two types of social contradictions : those between ourselves and the enemy and those among the people. The two are totally different in nature.
annotation.summary: Socialist society faces two fundamentally different kinds of conflicts: antagonistic conflicts between the people and their enemies, and non-antagonistic conflicts among the people themselves.
annotation.explanation: Mao introduces his central theoretical innovation for socialist governance: separating hostile class antagonisms against counter-revolutionaries from internal disagreements and structural tensions among the working masses and their allies.
annotation.context: A socialist state must treat foreign-backed sabotage or armed counter-revolution differently from a workplace dispute or policy disagreement among ordinary workers.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotations.bookTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People
annotations.chapterTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People

annotation.targetText: The only way to settle questions of an ideological nature or controversial issues among the people is by the democratic method, the method of discussion, criticism, persuasion and education, and not by the method of coercion or repression.
annotation.summary: Ideological questions and debates among the people cannot be solved by force or administrative bans; they can only be resolved through open discussion, criticism, persuasion, and education.
annotation.explanation: Because ideological beliefs and questions of right and wrong among the people cannot be forced by decree, Mao insists on patient reasoning, debate, and the 'unity : criticism : unity' method.
annotation.context: Banning a mistaken viewpoint among workers without explaining why it is wrong only drives the idea underground, whereas open discussion builds genuine understanding.

annotations.chapterTitle: On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People

annotation.targetText: The class struggle between the proletariat and the bourgeoisie, the class struggle between the various political forces, and the class struggle between the proletariat and the bourgeoisie in the ideological field will still be protracted and tortuous and at times even very sharp.
annotation.summary: Even after socialist ownership is established, the ideological and political struggle between the working class and the bourgeoisie remains long, complex, and at times intense.
annotation.explanation: Even after private ownership of industry and land is largely socialized, bourgeois and petty-bourgeois worldviews persist for decades, requiring ongoing ideological struggle so capitalism is not restored.
annotation.context: In socialist countries, old habits of individualism, careerism, and market mentality continue to influence culture and policy long after factories are nationalized.

annotation.targetText: Revisionism, or Right opportunism, is a bourgeois trend of thought that is even more dangerous than dogmatism.
annotation.summary: Revisionism is a bourgeois ideological trend inside the socialist movement that is even more dangerous than dogmatism because it hollows out the core of Marxism from within.
annotation.explanation: Mao warns that while dogmatists apply Marxist phrases mechanically, revisionists pay lip-service to Marxism while attacking its core principles: materialist dialectics, party leadership, and the people's democratic dictatorship.
annotation.context: Political factions that use socialist rhetoric while dismantling public ownership and weakening working-class state power pave the way for capitalist restoration.

annotation.targetText: Social-Democrats regard religion as a private matter in relation to the state, but not in relation to themselves, not in relation to Marxism, and not in relation to the workers' party
annotation.summary: Religion as a private matter relative to the state, not the party: refuting opportunist distortions of the 1891 Erfurt Programme (which demanded state secularization, not party neutrality).
annotation.explanation: The 1891 Erfurt Programme of German Social-Democracy demanded that 'religion is a private matter.' Opportunist leaders distorted this clause to argue that the party itself should remain neutral toward religion. Lenin clarifies Engels's distinction: while the workers' party demands that the bourgeois state treat religion as a private matter (disestablishing state churches, ending clerical subsidies, and guaranteeing freedom of conscience), the party itself must never treat religion as a private matter, but must actively champion dialectical materialism and educate workers against religious ideology.

annotation.targetText: Political power, properly so called, is merely the organised power of one class for oppressing another.
annotation.summary: Political power is by definition one class organised to suppress another, and it loses that character once classes disappear.
annotation.explanation: Marx and Engels define the state through its class function. When class distinctions vanish and production is concentrated in the hands of the associated nation, public power loses its political character, anticipating the later idea of the withering away of the state.
annotation.context: Lenin quoted this passage in The State and Revolution to argue that a workers' state is a transitional form that prepares its own disappearance.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText: first step in the revolution by the working class is to raise the proletariat to the position of ruling class, to win the battle of democracy. The proletariat will use its political supremacy to wrest, by degrees, all capital from the bourgeoisie, to centralise all instruments of production in the hands of the State, i.e., of the proletariat organised as the ruling class;
annotation.summary: The first task of a workers' revolution is to win political power as a class and use the state to take over the means of production.
annotation.explanation: Here the Manifesto links democracy with proletarian rule: winning the battle of democracy means the majority class organised as the ruling class, then centralising capital in its hands. This is the seed of the later theory of the dictatorship of the proletariat.
annotation.context: The passage directly shapes later debates about whether socialism is reached through elections, insurrection, or a combination of the two.
topics: The State and Dictatorship of the Proletariat

annotation.targetText:
Although the working-day is not a fixed, but a fluent quantity,
it can, on the other hand, only vary within certain limits. The minimum
limit is, however, not determinable; of course, if we make the extension
line B; ‑C or the surplus-labour = 0, we have a minimum limit, i.e.,
the part of the day which the labourer must necessarily work for his own
maintenance. On the basis of capitalist production, however, this necessary
labour can form a part only of the working-day; the working-day itself
can never be reduced to this minimum. On the other hand, the working-day
has a maximum limit. It cannot be prolonged beyond a certain point. This
maximum limit is conditioned by two things. First, by the physical bounds
of labour-power. Within the 24 hours of the natural day a man can expend
only a definite quantity of his vital force. A horse, in like manner, can
only work from day to day, 8 hours. During part of the day this force must
rest, sleep; during another part the man has to satisfy other physical
needs, to feed, wash, and clothe himself. Besides these purely physical
limitations, the extension of the working-day encounters moral ones. The
labourer needs time for satisfying his intellectual and social wants, the
extent and number of which are conditioned by the general state of social
advancement. The variation of the working-day fluctuates, therefore, within
physical and social bounds. But both these limiting conditions are of a
very elastic nature, and allow the greatest latitude. So we find working-days
of 8, 10, 12, 14, 16, 18 hours, i.e., of the most different lengths.
annotation.summary: The working day has both physical limits (the body needs sleep and food) and moral limits (workers need education, social life, and leisure). Capital constantly pushes against both boundaries.

annotation.targetText:
A locomotive, for instance, consists of more than 5,000
independent parts. It cannot, however, serve as an example of the first
kind of genuine manufacture, for it is a structure produced by modern mechanical
industry. But a watch can; and William Petty used it to illustrate the
division of labour in manufacture. Formerly the individual work of a Nuremberg
artificer, the watch has been transformed into the social product of an
immense number of detail labourers, such as mainspring makers, dial makers,
spiral spring makers, jewelled hole makers, ruby lever makers, hand makers,
case makers, screw makers, gilders, with numerous subdivisions, such as
wheel makers (brass and steel separate), pin makers, movement makers, acheveur
de pignon (fixes the wheels on the axles, polishes the facets, &c.),
pivot makers, planteur de finissage (puts the wheels and springs in the
works), finisseur de barillet (cuts teeth in the wheels, makes the holes
of the right size, &c.), escapement makers, cylinder makers for cylinder
escapements, escapement wheel makers, balance wheel makers, raquette makers
(apparatus for regulating the watch), the planteur d'échappement
(escapement maker proper); then the repasseur de barillet (finishes the
box for the spring, &c.), steel polishers, wheel polishers, screw polishers,
figure painters, dial enamellers (melt the enamel on the copper), fabricant
de pendants (makes the ring by which the case is hung), finisseur de charnière
(puts the brass hinge in the cover, &c.), faiseur de secret (puts in
the springs that open the case), graveur, ciseleur, polisseur de bo�te,
&c., &c., and last of all the repasseur, who fits together the
whole watch and hands it over in a going state. Only a few parts of the
watch pass through several hands; and all these membra disjecta come together
for the first time in the hand that binds them into one mechanical whole.
This external relation between the finished product, and its various and
diverse elements makes it, as well in this case as in the case of all similar
finished articles, a matter of chance whether the detail labourers are
brought together in one workshop or not. The detail operations may further
be carried on like so many independent handicrafts, as they are in the
Cantons of Vaud and Neufchâtel; while in Geneva there exist large
watch manufactories where the detail labourers directly co-operate under
the control of a single capitalist. And even in the latter case the dial, the springs, and the case, are seldom made in the factory itself. To carry
on the trade as a manufacture, with concentration of workmen, is, in the
watch trade, profitable only under exceptional conditions, because competition
is greater between the labourers who desire to work at home, and because
the splitting up of the work into a number of heterogeneous processes,
permits but little use of the instruments of labour in common, and the
capitalist, by scattering the work, saves the outlay on workshops,
&c. [7] Nevertheless the position of this detail
labourer who, though he works at home, does so for a capitalist (manufacturer,
établisseur), is very different from that of the independent artificer,
who works for his own customers. [8]
annotation.summary: Under manufacture, each worker performs only one tiny fraction of the total production process. This "detail laborer" becomes extremely skilled at their single task but loses the ability to produce a complete product independently.

annotation.targetText: The Catholic church was, at the time of the Reformation, feudal proprietor of a great part of the English land. The suppression of the monasteries, &c., hurled their inmates into the proletariat. The estates of the church were to a large extent given away to rapacious royal favourites, or sold at a nominal price to speculating farmers and citizens, who drove out, en masse, the hereditary sub-tenants and threw their holdings into one. The legally guaranteed property of the poorer folk in a part of the church's tithes was tacitly confiscated. [7] "Pauper ubique jacet," cried Queen Elizabeth, after a journey through England. In the 43rd year of her reign the nation was obliged to recognise pauperism officially by the introduction of a poor-rate. "The authors of this law seem to have been ashamed to state the grounds of it, for [contrary to traditional usage] it has no preamble whatever." [8] By the 16th of Charles I., ch. 4, it was declared perpetual, and in fact only in 1834 did it take a new and harsher form. [9] These immediate results of the Reformation were not its most lasting ones. The property of the church formed the religious bulwark of the traditional conditions of landed property. With its fall these were no longer tenable. [10] Even in the last decade of the 17th century, the yeomanry, the class of independent peasants, were more numerous than the class of farmers. They had formed the backbone of Cromwell's strength, and, even according to the confession of Macaulay, stood in favourable contrast to the drunken squires and to their servants, the country clergy, who had to marry their masters' cast-off mistresses. About 1750, the yeomanry had disappeared, [11] and so had, in the last decade of the 18th century, the last trace of the common land of the agricultural labourer. We leave on one side here the purely economic causes of the agricultural revolution. We deal only with the forcible means employed. After the restoration of the Stuarts, the landed proprietors carried, by legal means, an act of usurpation, effected everywhere on the Continent without any legal formality. They abolished the feudal tenure of land, i.e., they got rid of all its obligations to the State, "indemnified" the State by taxes on the peasantry and the rest of the mass of the people, vindicated for themselves the rights of modern private property in estates to which they had only a feudal title, and, finally, passed those laws of settlement, which, mutatis mutandis, had the same effect on the English agricultural labourer, as the edict of the Tartar Boris Godunof on the Russian peasantry. The "glorious Revolution" brought into power, along with William of Orange, the landlord and capitalist appropriators of surplus-value. [12] They inaugurated the new era by practising on a colossal scale thefts of state lands, thefts that had been hitherto managed more modestly. These estates were given away, sold at a ridiculous figure, or even annexed to private estates by direct seizure. [13] All this happened without the slightest observation of legal etiquette. The Crown lands thus fraudulently appropriated, together with the robbery of the Church estates, as far as these had not been lost again during the republican revolution, form the basis of the today princely domains of the English oligarchy. [14] The bourgeois capitalists favoured the operation with the view, among others, to promoting free trade in land, to extending the domain of modern agriculture on the large farm-system, and to increasing their supply of the free agricultural proletarians ready to hand. Besides, the new landed aristocracy was the natural ally of the new bankocracy, of the newly-hatched haute finance, and of the large manufacturers, then depending on protective duties. The English bourgeoisie acted for its own interest quite as wisely as did the Swedish bourgeoisie who, reversing the process, hand in hand with their economic allies, the peasantry, helped the kings in the forcible resumption of the Crown lands from the oligarchy. This happened since 1604 under Charles X. and Charles XI. Communal property ; always distinct from the State property just dealt with ; was an old Teutonic institution which lived on under cover of feudalism. We have seen how the forcible usurpation of this, generally accompanied by the turning of arable into pasture land, begins at the end of the 15th and extends into the 16th century. But, at that time, the process was carried on by means of individual acts of violence against which legislation, for a hundred and fifty years, fought in vain. The advance made by the 18th century shows itself in this, that the law itself becomes now the instrument of the theft of the people's land, although the large farmers make use of their little independent methods as well. [15] The parliamentary form of the robbery is that of Acts for enclosures of Commons, in other words, decrees by which the landlords grant themselves the people's land as private property, decrees of expropriation of the people. Sir F. M. Eden refutes his own crafty special pleading, in which he tries to represent communal property as the private property of the great landlords who have taken the place of the feudal lords, when he, himself, demands a "general Act of Parliament for the enclosure of Commons" (admitting thereby that a parliamentary coup d'état is necessary for its transformation into private property), and moreover calls on the legislature for the indemnification for the expropriated poor. [16] Whilst the place of the independent yeoman was taken by tenants at will, small farmers on yearly leases, a servile rabble dependent on the pleasure of the landlords, the systematic robbery of the Communal lands helped especially, next to the theft of the State domains, to swell those large farms, that were called in the 18th century capital farms [17] or merchant farms, [18] and to "set free" the agricultural population as proletarians for manufacturing industry. The 18th century, however, did not yet recognise as fully as the 19th, the identity between national wealth and the poverty of the people. Hence the most vigorous polemic, in the economic literature of that time, on the "enclosure of commons." From the mass of materials that lie before me, I give a few extracts that will throw a strong light on the circumstances of the time. "In several parishes of Hertfordshire," writes one indignant person, "24 farms, numbering on the average 50-150 acres, have been melted up into three farms." [19] "In Northamptonshire and Leicestershire the enclosure of common lands has taken place on a very large scale, and most of the new lordships, resulting from the enclosure, have been turned into pasturage, in consequence of which many lordships have not now 50 acres ploughed yearly, in which 1,500 were ploughed formerly. The ruins of former dwelling-houses, barns, stables, &c.," are the sole traces of the former inhabitants. "An hundred houses and families have in some open-field villages dwindled to eight or ten.... The landholders in most parishes that have been enclosed only 15 or 20 years, are very few in comparison of the numbers who occupied them in their open-field state. It is no uncommon thing for 4 or 5 wealthy graziers to engross a large enclosed lordship which was before in the hands of 20 or 30 farmers, and as many smaller tenants and proprietors. All these are hereby thrown out of their livings with their families and many other families who were chiefly employed and supported by them." [20] It was not only the land that lay waste, but often land cultivated either in common or held under a definite rent paid to the community, that was annexed by the neighbouring landlords under pretext of enclosure. "I have here in view enclosures of open fields and lands already improved. It is acknowledged by even the writers in defence of enclosures that these diminished villages increase the monopolies of farms, raise the prices of provisions, and produce depopulation ... and even the enclosure of waste lands (as now carried on) bears hard on the poor, by depriving them of a part of their subsistence, and only goes towards increasing farms already too large." [21] "When," says Dr. Price, "this land gets into the hands of a few great farmers, the consequence must be that the little farmers" (earlier designated by him "a multitude of little proprietors and tenants, who maintain themselves and families by the produce of the ground they occupy by sheep kept on a common, by poultry, hogs, &c., and who therefore have little occasion to purchase any of the means of subsistence") "will be converted into a body of men who earn their subsistence by working for others, and who will be under a necessity of going to market for all they want.... There will, perhaps, be more labour, because there will be more compulsion to it.... Towns and manufactures will increase, because more will be driven to them in quest of places and employment. This is the way in which the engrossing of farms naturally operates. And this is the way in which, for many years, it has been actually operating in this kingdom." [22] He sums up the effect of the enclosures thus: "Upon the whole, the circumstances of the lower ranks of men are altered in almost every respect for the worse. From little occupiers of land, they are reduced to the state of day-labourers and hirelings; and, at the same time, their subsistence in that state has become more difficult." [23] In fact, usurpation of the common lands and the revolution in agriculture accompanying this, told so acutely on the agricultural labourers that, even according to Eden, between 1765 and 1780, their wages began to fall below the minimum, and to be supplemented by official poor-law relief. Their wages, he says, "were not more than enough for the absolute necessaries of life." Let us hear for a moment a defender of enclosures and an opponent of Dr. Price. "Not is it a consequence that there must be depopulation, because men are not seen wasting their labour in the open field.... If, by converting the little farmers into a body of men who must work for others, more labour is produced, it is an advantage which the nation" (to which, of course, the "converted" ones do not belong) "should wish for ... the produce being greater when their joint labours are employed on one farm, there will be a surplus for manufactures, and by this means manufactures, one of the mines of the nation, will increase, in proportion to the quantity of corn produced." [24] The stoical peace of mind with which the political economist regards the most shameless violation of the "sacred rights of property" and the grossest acts of violence to persons, as soon as they are necessary to lay the foundations of the capitalistic mode of production, is shown by Sir F. M. Eden, philanthropist and tory to boot. The whole series of thefts, outrages, and popular misery, that accompanied the forcible expropriation of the people, from the last third of the 15th to the end of the 18th century, lead him merely to the comfortable conclusion: "The due proportion between arable land and pasture had to be established. During the whole of the 14th and the greater part of the 15th century, there was one acre of pasture to 2, 3, and even 4 of arable land. About the middle of the 16th century the proportion was changed of 2 acres of pasture to 2, later on, of 2 acres of pasture to one of arable, until at last the just proportion of 3 acres of pasture to one of arable land was attained." In the 19th century, the very memory of the connexion between the agricultural labourer and the communal property had, of course, vanished. To say nothing of more recent times, have the agricultural population received a farthing of compensation for the 3,511,770 acres of common land which between 1801 and 1831 were stolen from them and by parliamentary devices presented to the landlords by the landlords? The last process of wholesale expropriation of the agricultural population from the soil is, finally, the so-called clearing of estates, i.e., the sweeping men off them. All the English methods hitherto considered culminated in "clearing." As we saw in the picture of modern conditions given in a former chapter, where there are no more independent peasants to get rid of, the "clearing" of cottages begins; so that the agricultural labourers do not find on the soil cultivated by them even the spot necessary for their own housing. But what "clearing of estates" really and properly signifies, we learn only in the promised land of modern romance, the Highlands of Scotland. There the process is distinguished by its systematic character, by the magnitude of the scale on which it is carried out at one blow (in Ireland landlords have gone to the length of sweeping away several villages at once; in Scotland areas as large as German principalities are dealt with), finally by the peculiar form of property, under which the embezzled lands were held. The Highland Celts were organised in clans, each of which was the owner of the land on which it was settled. The representative of the clan, its chief or "great man," was only the titular owner of this property, just as the Queen of England is the titular owner of all the national soil. When the English government succeeded in suppressing the intestine wars of these "great men," and their constant incursions into the Lowland plains, the chiefs of the clans by no means gave up their time-honored trade as robbers; they only changed its form. On their own authority they transformed their nominal right into a right of private property, and as this brought them into collision with their clansmen, resolved to drive them out by open force. "A king of England might as well claim to drive his subjects into the sea," says Professor Newman. [25] This revolution, which began in Scotland after the last rising of the followers of the Pretender, can be followed through its first phases in the writings of Sir James Steuart [26] and James Anderson. [27] In the 18th century the hunted-out Gaels were forbidden to emigrate from the country, with a view to driving them by force to Glasgow and other manufacturing towns. [28] As an example of the method [29] obtaining in the 19th century, the "clearing" made by the Duchess of Sutherland will suffice here. This person, well instructed in economy, resolved, on entering upon her government, to effect a radical cure, and to turn the whole country, whose population had already been, by earlier processes of the like kind, reduced to 15,000, into a sheep-walk. From 1814 to 1820 these 15,000 inhabitants, about 3,000 families, were systematically hunted and rooted out. All their villages were destroyed and burnt, all their fields turned into pasturage. British soldiers enforced this eviction, and came to blows with the inhabitants. One old woman was burnt to death in the flames of the hut, which she refused to leave. Thus this fine lady appropriated 794,000 acres of land that had from time immemorial belonged to the clan. She assigned to the expelled inhabitants about 6,000 acres on the sea-shore ; 2 acres per family. The 6,000 acres had until this time lain waste, and brought in no income to their owners. The Duchess, in the nobility of her heart, actually went so far as to let these at an average rent of 2s. 6d. per acre to the clansmen, who for centuries had shed their blood for her family. The whole of the stolen clanland she divided into 29 great sheep farms, each inhabited by a single family, for the most part imported English farm-servants. In the year 1835 the 15,000 Gaels were already replaced by 131,000 sheep. The remnant of the aborigines flung on the sea-shore tried to live by catching fish. They became amphibious and lived, as an English author says, half on land and half on water, and withal only half on both. [30] But the brave Gaels must expiate yet more bitterly their idolatry, romantic and of the mountains, for the "great men" of the clan. The smell of their fish rose to the noses of the great men. They scented some profit in it, and let the sea-shore to the great fishmongers of London. For the second time the Gaels were hunted out. [31] But, finally, part of the sheep-walks are turned into deer preserves. Every one knows that there are no real forests in England. The deer in the parks of the great are demurely domestic cattle, fat as London aldermen. Scotland is therefore the last refuge of the "noble passion." "In the Highlands," says Somers in 1848, "new forests are springing up like mushrooms. Here, on one side of Gaick, you have the new forest of Glenfeshie; and there on the other you have the new forest of Ardverikie. In the same line you have the Black Mount, an immense waste also recently erected. From east to west ; from the neighbourhood of Aberdeen to the crags of Oban ; you have now a continuous line of forests; while in other parts of the Highlands there are the new forests of Loch Archaig, Glengarry, Glenmoriston, &c. Sheep were introduced into glens which had been the seats of communities of small farmers; and the latter were driven to seek subsistence on coarser and more sterile tracks of soil. Now deer are supplanting sheep; and these are once more dispossessing the small tenants, who will necessarily be driven down upon still coarser land and to more grinding penury. Deer-forests [32] and the people cannot co-exist. One or other of the two must yield. Let the forests be increased in number and extent during the next quarter of a century, as they have been in the last, and the Gaels will perish from their native soil... This movement among the Highland proprietors is with some a matter of ambition... with some love of sport... while others, of a more practical cast, follow the trade in deer with an eye solely to profit. For it is a fact, that a mountain range laid out in forest is, in many cases, more profitable to the proprietor than when let as a sheep-walk. ... The huntsman who wants a deer-forest limits his offers by no other calculation than the extent of his purse.... Sufferings have been inflicted in the Highlands scarcely less severe than those occasioned by the policy of the Norman kings. Deer have received extended ranges, while men have been hunted within a narrower and still narrower circle.... One after one the liberties of the people have been cloven down.... And the oppressions are daily on the increase.... The clearance and dispersion of the people is pursued by the proprietors as a settled principle, as an agricultural necessity, just as trees and brushwood are cleared from the wastes of America or Australia; and the operation goes on in a quiet, business-like way, &c." [33] The spoliation of the church's property, the fraudulent alienation of the State domains, the robbery of the common lands, the usurpation of feudal and clan property, and its transformation into modern private property under circumstances of reckless terrorism, were just so many idyllic methods of primitive accumulation. They conquered the field for capitalistic agriculture, made the soil part and parcel of capital, and created for the town industries the necessary supply of a "free" and outlawed proletariat.
annotation.summary: The violent enclosures and clearing of estates: how peasant land was expropriated to forge the industrial proletariat.
annotation.explanation: Through the seizure of monastic lands, fraudulent appropriation of state domains, and enclosure of village commons, rural populations were systematically dispossessed. Their eviction transformed agricultural land into commercial sheep pastures and herded millions of destitute people into urban wage slavery.

annotation.targetText: the whole of the 16th century, throughout Western Europe a bloody legislation against vagabondage. The fathers of the present working class were chastised for their enforced transformation into vagabonds and paupers. Legislation treated them as "voluntary" criminals, and assumed that it depended on their own good will to go on working under the old conditions that no longer existed.
annotation.summary: Bloody legislation against vagabondage: the state criminalizes the dispossessed peasantry to enforce wage labour.
annotation.explanation: Peasants driven from the land could not be absorbed into early manufactures quickly enough. The state stepped in with savage criminal statutes: whipping, branding with hot irons, and enslavement for vagrancy: coercing displaced rural populations into the brutal discipline required by emerging capital.

annotation.targetText: The bourgeoisie, at its rise, wants and uses the power of the state to "regulate" wages, i.e., to force them within the limits suitable for surplus-value making, to lengthen the working-day and to keep the labourer himself in the normal degree of dependence. This is an essential element of the so-called primitive accumulation.
annotation.summary: State regulation of wages: the rising bourgeoisie deploys state power to cap wages and prolong the working day.
annotation.explanation: Far from believing in free-market wage setting, the early capitalist class relied on state legislation to impose wage ceilings and penalize workers who demanded higher pay, ensuring a high rate of surplus-value extraction.

[Since we have assumed that commodities are bought and sold at
their values, these acts constitute merely the conversion of a certain
value from one form into another, from the commodity-form into the money-form
or from the money-form into the commodity-form ; a change in the state
of being. If commodities are sold at their values, then the magnitudes
of value in the hands of the buyer and seller remain unchanged. Only the
form of existence of value is changed. If the commodities are not sold
at their values, then the sum of the converted values remains unchanged;
the plus on one side is a minus on the other.
annotation.summary: Pure circulation costs (buying, selling, bookkeeping) do not create new value. If commodities sell at their values, value simply changes form from commodity to money or vice versa; no new wealth is produced in the act of exchange itself.

annotation.targetText:
We have laid bare three fundamental motives for the conquest policies of modern capitalist states: increased competition in the sales markets, in the markets of raw materials, and for the spheres of capital investment. This is what the modern development of capitalism and its transformation into finance capitalism has brought about.

Those three roots of the policy of finance capitalism, however, represent in substance only three facets of the same phenomenon, namely of the conflict between the growth of productive forces on the one hand, and the "national" limits of the production organisation on the other.
annotation.summary: The three drivers of imperialist conquest (sales markets, raw materials, and capital investment spheres) stem from the conflict between global productive forces and national bourgeois states.
annotation.explanation: Bukharin synthesizes his theory of imperialism: productive forces have outgrown the narrow framework of the nation-state, forcing finance capital to attempt to resolve the contradiction through military conquest.

annotation.summary: Eliminating competition among small firms inside a nation intensifies destructive competition among giant state-capitalist trusts on the world stage.
annotation.explanation: Instead of competing merely through lower prices, state-capitalist trusts deploy tariffs, credit blockades, raw material boycotts, and military force to crush foreign rivals.

annotation.summary: Imperialist world war acts as a gigantic crisis that destroys productive forces while vastly accelerating finance-capitalist centralization and state capitalism.
annotation.explanation: Bukharin documents how World War I wiped out small enterprises, subordinated entire national economies to state-capitalist war syndicates, and propelled the United States to global financial supremacy.
